thread.title: Intraday Update: Dow Jumps 170 Points Because Who Needs Tech Anyway?

author: Crystal Kim
title: Intraday Update: Dow Jumps 170 Points Because Who Needs Tech Anyway?
text:
By Crystal Kim July 24, 2018 1:21 p.m. ET Google It . Markets appeared to have found what they were searching for in Alphabet 's (GOOGL) earnings results , as the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose above its mid-July high. President Donald Trump expects U.S. gross domestic product growth to impress, too. In today's Intraday Update, we...
Illustration: Getty Images •...bust one market myth;
•...wonder if growth will continue to beat the tar out of value;
•...see Harley-Davidson (HOG) is one uneasy rider when it comes to tariffs.
The Skinny We're seeing something we haven't seen in a while–the Dow Jones Industrial Average outperforming the other major indexes.
The Dow has risen 0.7% to 25,221.05. While the S&P 500 has gained 0.5% to 2822.21 and the Nasdaq Composite is flat at around 7839.67.
With Facebook (FB), Apple (AAPL), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet doing a lot of the heavy lifting recently , a chorus of investors have touted the "narrow market" argument to call a top and, of course, the eventual downturn. The fact that the Nasdaq hasn't been able to hold on to its gains will probably just add fuel to the fire.
But the idea that the biggest stocks in the S&P 500 make up a much too large a weighting in the broad index is a myth, writes Ned Davis Research Group 's chief U.S. strategist Ed Clissold . True, the five biggest stocks in the S&P 500 has jumped to 14% at the end of June from 10% in April 2016, but the biggest stocks have always had a higher weight than constituents in the bottom half. "Since 1972, the average weight of the top five stocks has been 14.3% versus 11.7% for the bottom half. The bottom half's current weight of 13.7% is only 0.8% below the record high set in June 2014," says Clissold.
What is concerning: Relatively few stocks are making new 52-week highs despite the S&P 500 not being that far from its record. Of the stocks in Clissold's multi-cap universe only 12% made fresh 52-week highs compared to 38% in January.
Illustration: Getty Images But maybe that's starting to change. While technology stocks have been dominant, otherwise U.S.-focused businesses are breaking out. Retail , transportation, and more recently financials (e.g. banks) are leading the way. The Financial Select Sector SPDR exchange-traded fund (XLF) notched its third one-percent gain in the last six trading sessions . The big question is, as always: Where is it headed next? Financial stocks seem to be in a holding pattern of gain and retreat. In the last few months, the ETF's strength has faded after reaching current levels, but if the broad market is eyeing a new high, financial stocks will to show up and continue to show up.
The one big thing investors should watch is rather small. The relative performance of growth stocks to value has been less robust in small caps than it has been in the mid- and large caps. That's a trend to watch, because weakness in small companies led to weakness in large companies in 2015. "Look at the small caps and their progression from 2015: Small-cap stocks stalled out before midcap, and midcap before large," Robert Sluymer , Fundstrat technical strategist told Barron's, "I'd be more worried if small-cap growth's relative performance to small-cap value undershoots the low established in April and May."
Clissold says value stocks' best shot at sustained outperformance is accelerating economic growth, Fed normalization or the market goes full on bear. Perhaps there's hope for the first since President Trump seems to think U.S. GDP growth will roll in at greater than 4.8%, higher than the top of consensus expectations for 4.3% to 4.4%.
We'll find out on Friday.
